1.1 How to use this repository ?

1.1.1 Repository organisation
The git repository linked to this website is available here and is saved via SoftwareHeritage on this page.
Folders containing files concerning directly the study :

data folder : Contains the raw data files with direct notations from the experiments
functions folder : Contains R scripts with general functions used throughout different scripts
quarto folder : Contains all the .qmd files that generate the html pages, and their associated cache and files which cannot be moved to another folder.
mod folder : Contain all the models generated in .rds files
bootstrap folder : Contain the R script and its results concerning the bootstrap.
photos folder : Contains all photos used in html pages
fig folder : Contains all figure generated by quarto documents
references folder

apa.csl : File of the reference style used for the website
reference.bib : File containing all references from a zotero library


Folders concerning the setup of the git repository and the web pages :

_book : Where the final html pages are created
index.qmd : Home page of the web site (cannot be put in the quarto folder)
_quarto.yaml : YAML file that setup the structure of the website from the quarto (.qmd) documents
_freeze folder : Cache the results of code blocks (code cells) to avoid recalculating them on each execution
.git, .gitignore & .github : Git related folders
.quarto : Store configuration files, metadata, and intermediate files related to a Quarto project
.Rproj.user & Ew-Mix-TD.Rproj : R project related files
appearance folder :

html_css.scss : CSS file to modify the look of the html pages
lightnord.theme : Theme to use for code blocks displayed in the html pages




1.1.2 How to reproduce everything
If you wish to reproduce the results of this study, all you need are available in the quarto folder and the mod folder.
Instructions :

Whether or not you want to run the models again, please delete the folders from the quarto folder that end by _cache or _files and delete all the figures present in the fig folder.

If you do not want to run the models again, move on to the next step
If you wish to run the models again, please delete the files in mod but the .model files and keep the arborescence)

Then, you can render again all .qmd files from the quarto folder in the alphabetical order of their name. Some code line will have to be de-commented for some figures to be rendered again.

2.1.1 Earthworm model - Aporrectodea caliginosa
Aporrectodea caliginosa (Figure 2.1), an endogeic earthworm species, was the chosen biological model for it is considered highly representative of agricultural soil (Bart, 2018) and is part of the most sensitive agricultural species to pesticides (Pelosi et al., 2013). It is also a species we are able to cultivate under laboratory conditions (Section 2.1.1.1).






Figure 2.1: Adult A. caliginosa individual.




2.1.1.1 Earthworm cultivation at EcoSys
A further objective of the project this study is part of is to evaluate the effects of a pesticides mixture on inter-individual variations of life-history traits and behavior of A. caliginosa. To achieve this, it is essential to use individuals whose genetic diversity is representative of a natural population with limited exposure to plant protection products (PPPs). This excludes the use of the breeding stock maintained at EcoSys, as the individuals have been kept in a closed system since the initiation of the breeding program (for over 5 years), with no consideration for maintaining genetic diversity. Therefore, it was necessary to establish a new A. caliginosa breeding population appropriate for the scientific questions addressed in this study.


2.1.1.2 Initially collected individuals.
To initiate the culture, individuals were collected from a natural population in a permanent grassland in Versailles (48°48′ N, 2°5′ E, called “les Closeaux”) where no pesticides have been applied for more than 25 years (Figure 2.2). The individuals were identified using a binocular microscope and an identification key. Ten sampling sessions were conducted in the fall of 2023 and the spring of 2024, yielding a total of 325 individuals.






Figure 2.2: Collection of Aporrectodea caliginosa and Aporrectodea icterica individuals in a meadow at the Château de Versailles and installation of the new culture in our laboratory.




2.1.1.2.1 Workflow
Individuals are bred at 18°C in 1 L vessels in groups of five individuals (Figure 2.2) using a loamy soil texture called Closeaux soil (based on the texture definition of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)), sampled from the same meadow as initial individuals. Pesticides found in the soil are summarized in Figure 2.3 and its general properties in Table 2.1. The soil was collected from the top 0-20 cm, air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm mesh. Soil culture is kept with a soil water-holding capacity (WHC) of 60-70%. Individuals are fed with horse dung frost and defrosted twice before being milled (> 1mm) as presented in Lowe & Butt (2005). They are fed each month with the equivalent of around 6 g of dry horse dung which are given with a WHC of 60-70%.

title: 2  Earthworms and pesticides
text:
2.2 Pesticides of interest
Because our aim was to study a mixture of pesticides representative of earthworm exposure in agricultural soils, a crucial step of the study was to select two relevant pesticides.

2.2.1 Choice of Epoxiconazole and Imidacloprid
The selection was made in fall 2023 and was guided by two main criteria: the ubiquity and persistence of pesticide residues in soils, and the availability of ecotoxicological data on earthworms.
Froger et al. (2023) conducted an extensive nationwide survey of pesticide contamination in French soils, monitoring 111 pesticide residues across 47 sites under various land uses. Epoxiconazole and imidacloprid were detected in 47% and 9% of all sites, respectively, with median concentrations of 5.8 ng/g and 2.9 ng/g, and maximum concentrations of 23.6 ng/g and 13.8 ng/g. In arable lands, epoxiconazole, bixafen, fluopyram, fluxapyroxad, glyphosate & AMPA, diflufenican, and terfluthrin were among the most frequently detected compounds.
In a complementary study, Pelosi et al. (2021) investigated the exposure of earthworms to 31 pesticide residues in both treated and untreated habitats within an intensive agricultural landscape in France (Spring 2016, Long-Term Socio-Ecological Research Site, Zone Atelier Plaine & Val de Sèvre). Diflufenican, imidacloprid, boscalid, and epoxiconazole were among the most frequently detected residues, found in more than 80% of sampled soils.
Based on these two studies, we initially targeted a range of pesticide residues. Ultimately, we selected epoxiconazole and imidacloprid due to the availability of toxicological data and their known effects on earthworms (Bart et al., 2019, 2020; Capowiez et al., 2006; Dittbrenner et al., 2010, 2011; Pelosi et al., 2016; Van Loon et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019). Despite being now banned in the EU, both pesticides continue to be of concern due to their ubiquity and persistence in the environment. These pesticides have been shown to persist in agricultural soils, with concentrations that can still pose adverse effects on non-target organisms, such as earthworms. Imidacloprid is particularly known for impairing earthworm bioturbation, a critical process that supports many ecosystem functions (Chen et al., 2021). Both pesticides’ enduring presence in the environment highlights the relevance of studying their long-term ecological impacts. This choice aligns with the objectives of the EEWORM ANR project, which aims to investigate the eco-evolutionary dynamics of earthworms under pesticide exposure and the resulting impacts on ecosystem functions.

2.2.2 Epoxiconazole (EPX)
Epoxiconazole (EPX) is a broad-spectrum fungicide from the azole family, used to control plant diseases caused by Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, and Deuteromycetes (Lewis et al., 2006). It was commercialized by BASF SE in 1993 and applied to a variety of crops including cereals, soy, bananas, rice, coffee, beets, and turnips (Lewis et al., 2006). Epoxiconazole has also been investigated for medical applications due to its antifungal properties, although its primary use has remained agricultural (Hamdi et al., 2022).
In France, EPX was widely applied on cultivated land, primarily as a foliar treatment. Before its withdrawal, approximately 200 tons were sold annually. Its market authorization was revoked by ANSES in 2019, and subsequently at the EU level in 2020.
Epoxiconazole is a sterol biosynthesis inhibitor (SBI) (Lewis et al., 2006). It disrupts fungal metabolism by inhibiting mycelial growth, reducing conidia production, and limiting mycotoxin synthesis. Like other triazole fungicides, its main mode of action is the inhibition of cytochrome P450 14α-demethylase (CYP51), a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of sterols such as ergosterol (Vanden Bossche et al., 1990; Zarn et al., 2003). Ergosterol is an essential component of fungal cell membranes, and its disruption compromises fungal viability.
Beyond its antifungal activity, EPX has been shown to interact with endocrine pathways. It acts as an androgen receptor agonist and promotes the synthesis of sex steroid hormones in vitro, which can interfere with developmental processes and individual growth (Kjærstad et al., 2010; Zarn et al., 2003). EPX also showed to be carcinogenic on rats. EPX is therefore considered as a reprotoxic and a suspected carcenogenic (echa_2025b?).
The half-life of epoxiconazole is 353.5 days in soil (20°C), 103.4 days in water-sediment (20°C) and 1000 days in water only (20°C) (Lewis et al., 2006), which makes it a very persistant substance in the environment. Its logK\(_{ow}\) above 3 makes it likely to bind to the organic matter in soil. Overall, there is broad agreement in that this substance is Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic (PBT) (echa_2025b?).
On earthworms, epoxiconazole impacts growth, maturation and reproduction (Bart et al., 2019, 2020). In field studies, it was shown to reduce the species diversity, anecic abundance and total biomass (Amossé et al., 2020).

2.2.3 Imidacloprid (IMD)
Imidacloprid (IMD) is a systemic insecticide belonging to the chloronicotinyl (neonicotinoid) family. It is widely used in agriculture across the globe to control sap-feeding insects such as plant hoppers, aphids, termites, Colorado potato beetles, fleas, white grubs, craneflies, crickets, and ants (Lewis et al., 2006). Its applications included lawns and turf, as well as crops such as rice, cereals, maize, potatoes, and sugar beet. It was also used in veterinary medicine, notably in flea treatments for domestic pets. Imidacloprid was commercialized by Bayer in 1991 (Lewis et al., 2006).
In France, the use of neonicotinoids — including imidacloprid — was progressively restricted following the adoption of the 2016 law on the “reconquest of biodiversity, nature and landscapes” (loi pour la reconquête de la biodiversité, de la nature et des paysages). The European Union withdrew the market authorization for imidacloprid in 2020. Currently, only acetamiprid remains approved for use in France and the EU, primarily for veterinary purposes. A temporary derogation had allowed the use of imidacloprid and thiamethoxam for aphid-infested beet crops, but this exemption was definitively revoked in January 2023, reinforcing the ban on neonicotinoids following multiple regulatory actions at both French and European levels (anses_2020?).
Imidacloprid exerts its toxic effects by acting as an agonist of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), leading to overstimulation and subsequent disruption of the central nervous system in target invertebrates (Chen et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2006). This mechanism makes it highly effective at low concentrations, but also raises concerns about its non-target effects, particularly on soil invertebrates such as earthworms.
Imidacloprid is also under assessment for endocrine disrupting (echa_2025b?).
The half-life of imidacloprid is 2.3 years in fresh water (12°C), 1.1 years in freshwater-sediment (12°C) and 1.4 years in soil (12°C) (Lewis et al., 2006), which makes it a very persistant substance in the environment.
On earthworms, imidacloprid significatively impacts survival but also growth, maturation and reproduction (Dittbrenner et al., 2011; Pelosi et al., 2016; Van Loon et al., 2022). It was also shown to disturbe activities of carboxylesterase (CarE) and glutathione-S- transferases (GST) (Wang et al., 2019). More importantly, it affects earthworms’ burrowing activity, essential for the various ecosystem functions endorsed by earthworms (Capowiez et al., 2006; Dittbrenner et al., 2010).

2.2.4 Environmental concentrations
Recent monitoring data from French agricultural soils reveal substantial variability in pesticide residue levels. Froger et al. (2023) reported imidacloprid concentrations with median values of 2.9 ng/g (0.0029 mg/kg), reaching maximum concentrations of 13.8 ng/g (0.0138 mg/kg) and third quartile values of 5.8 ng/g (0.0058 mg/kg). Epoxiconazole concentrations were higher, with median concentrations of 5.8 ng/g (0.0058 mg/kg), maximum values of 23.6 ng/g (0.0236 mg/kg), and third quartile concentrations of 10.9 ng/g (0.0109 mg/kg). More comprehensive surveys focusing on conventional cereal farming systems show elevated contamination levels (Pelosi et al., 2021). Imidacloprid median concentrations reached 15.1 ng/g (0.0151 mg/kg) with maximum values of 160 ng/g (0.16 mg/kg), while epoxiconazole showed median concentrations of 34.6 ng/g (0.0346 mg/kg) with maximum values of 283 ng/g (0.283 mg/kg). These concentrations can be contextualized against recommended application doses of 168 ng/g for imidacloprid and 153 ng/g for epoxiconazole (Pelosi et al., 2021). Environmental residue levels show that soil contamination can reach substantial fractions of recommended doses, with maximum detected concentrations representing 95% (160/168) of the recommended dose for imidacloprid and 185% (283/153) for epoxiconazole. Median concentrations in conventional cereal farming represent 9% and 23% of recommended doses for imidacloprid and epoxiconazole, respectively.

title: 3  Experimental design
text:
3.1 Soil contamination
Our experimental designs are based on OECD TG 222 about reproduction tests performed on earthworms. A summary of the procedure is given in this section but detailled protocols are available in the protocols folder.
All experiments were performed at 18°C with a soil from a permanent grassland in Versailles (48°48′ N, 2°5′ E, called “les Closeaux”) where no pesticides have been applied for more than 25 years. More information is available Section 2.1. Individuals were always fed with 3 g/ind/14 days (ad libitum conditions). Soil humidity is checked and adjusted every week. At the end of the experiments, earthworms are starved to empty their gut content on wet filter paper in Petri dishes before being frozen at -80°C.
Pesticides concentrations were chosen thanks to preliminary tests presented Section 3.4.
The contamination of soil was performed a day prior to the beginning of the experiment. Due to the very low water solubility of epoxiconazole and the relatively high tested concentrations, it was not possible to spike the soil with a water solution containing epoxiconazole. The alternative use of a co-solvent was avoided, as they are often toxic to earthworms, and the required quantity would have been excessive. One day prior to the start of the tests, the soil contamination was carried out depending on the substance : a dry mixture of epoxiconazole and soil at 20% of its WHC with an addition of water to adjust the soil WHC to 70% ; a spiking the soil with a water solution of imidacloprid with an addition of water to adjust the soil WHC to 70%. The soil isn’t mixed until the morning after on the start of the experiment.

3.3 Reproduction experiments


Code
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("photos/Reproduction_experiment_design.png")) 





Experimental design of the reproduction experiments




For each replicate, two earthworms are placed in a cosm made of a plastic vessel (11 cm x 7.7 cm x 4.5 cm) containing the equivalent of 200 g of dry soil for 28 days. Individuals are weighted at the beginning and the end of the experiment. Cocoons produced during the experiment are retrieved by wet sieving the soil through a 1-mm mesh size (Bart, 2018), and incubated at 18°C in Petri dishes on wet filter papers (Holmstrup et al., 1991). Cocoon hatching is monitored over the next four weeks.
As nothing ever goes according to plan, the cocoon hatling monitoring could not be properly done as a power shortage disrupted the temperature of our incubator.

title: 3  Experimental design
text:
3.4 Preliminary tests
Preliminary tests were performed to identify the concentration range capturing the whole range of effect of each substance. This would allow us to choose more carrefully the tested concentrations for each substance.

3.4.1 Method
At the time of these preliminary tests, our lab culture had just started and thus we could not use A. caliginosa from our lab. In the Closeaux meadow, A. icterica were easy to find so we chose to performed the test with these collected individuals.
These tests were performed as described above with the difference being that juveniles were put by 2 instead of 1 in cosms. Growth tests were performed in 1 replicate and reproduction tests were performed in 2 replicates.
The tested concentrations are the following :

IMD : 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 mg/kg
EPX : 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 mg/kg



3.4.2 Results

3.4.2.1 Variables names

Date : Date of the measurement
ID : Identification number of the earthworm
ID_cosm : Identification number of the cosm
t : Number of days since the start of the exposition
w : Fresh weight of the earthworm (mg)
w_tot : Fresh weight of the earthworms in one cosm (mg)
nb_ind : Number of individuals in one cosm (#)
Dose : concentration in the soil (mg/kg)
Status :

“J” : Juvenile
“A” : Adulte
“D” : Dead

Figure 3.1: Juvenile earthworms growth.





Earthworms growth can be modeled thanks to Equation 3.1.
\[\frac{dL}{dt}=a \Rightarrow L(t)=L_0 = a\times t \tag{3.1}\]
With :

L : The structural volumetric length of the earthworm (\(= \sqrt[3]{w}\)) (mg\(^{1/3}\))
a : Growth rate (mg\(^{1/3}\)/d)

For each earthworm, the growth rate is estimated using the “deSolve” package.


Code
a_init <- 0.1

df_rates <- data.frame(
  ID = df_growth[df_growth$t==0,]$ID,
  Dose = df_growth[df_growth$t==0,]$Dose,
  Molecule = df_growth[df_growth$t==0,]$Molecule
  )
a_i <- c()

for(i in df_growth[df_growth$t==0,]$ID){
  
  data_i <- data.frame(
    L=df_growth[df_growth$ID==i,]$L,
    t=df_growth[df_growth$ID==i,]$t
    )
  L0_i <- df_growth[df_growth$ID==i & df_growth$t==0,]$L
  
  mod.nlsHill=nls(
    L ~ L0_i+t*a,
    start = list(a=a_init), 
    trace=T, 
    data=data_i
    ) 
  
  a.Est=mod.nlsHill$m$getPars()[1]
  a_i <- c(a_i, a.Est)
}

df_rates <- df_rates%>%
  mutate(a_i=a_i)%>%
  mutate(Status=df_growth[df_growth$t>=28,]$Status)

df_rates$a_i <- replace_na(df_rates$a_i, 0)

df_rates_alive <- df_rates[!df_rates$Status=="D",]

df_rates_alive_mean <- df_rates_alive |> 
  aggregate(a_i ~ Dose + Molecule, FUN=mean)

4  Effects of single exposures on earthworms

title: 4  Effects of single exposures on earthworms
text:
4.1.1 Reproduction experiments
Our earthworm breeding system is described Section 2.1.1.1.
The soil used for all experiments is the same as the culture to be as close as possible to the conditions of the natural population.
For all experiments, Imidacloprid PESTANAL®, analytical standard (ref 37894-100MG) and Epoxiconazole regarder flacon au N1 (ref ) from Sigma-Aldrich were used. Due to the very low water solubility of epoxiconazole and the relatively high tested concentrations, it was not possible to spike the soil with a water solution containing both epoxiconazole and imidacloprid. The alternative use of a co-solvent was avoided, as they are often toxic to earthworms, and the required quantity would have been excessive. One day prior to the start of the tests, the soil contamination was carried out in two stages: first, a dry mixture of epoxiconazole and soil at 20% of its WHC was prepared, followed by spiking the soil with a water solution of imidacloprid.
Reproduction tests were conducted following an adaptation of the OECD Technical Guideline 222 (OECD, 2016) in a two-stage experiment. Each pesticide was first tested individually (Experiment A) before assessing the mixture (Experiment B).
To study the effects of individual pesticides, tested concentrations were selected based on the ecotoxicological data from Lewis et al. (2006). For Eisenia fetida, the reported acute 14-day LC50 values were 10.7 mg/kg for imidacloprid and >500 mg/kg for epoxiconazole, while the chronic reproduction NOEC values were ≥3.24 mg/kg and ≥0.178 mg/kg, respectively. An initial set of eight concentrations was selected for each pesticide, arranged in a geometric sequence to cover the full response range. For imidacloprid, an additional set of three concentrations, including one already tested, was added to refine the dose-response curve. Each concentration was tested in five replicates.
For each replicate, two earthworms were placed in a cosm consisting of a plastic vessel (11 cm × 7.7 cm × 4.5 cm) containing the equivalent of 200 g of dry soil. The exposure lasted 28 days at 18°C. Earthworms were weighed at the start and end of the experiment and were fed ad libitum with horse dung (3 g per individual every 14 days).
Soil moisture was checked and adjusted weekly. At the end of the experiments, earthworms were starved on wet filter paper in Petri dishes to empty their gut contents before being frozen at -80°C. Cocoons produced during the experiments were retrieved by wet-sieving the soil through a 1-mm mesh (Bart, 2018) and incubated at 18°C in Petri dishes on wet filter paper (Holmstrup et al., 1991). Cocoon hatching was monitored each day of the working week for 96 days for imidacloprid and 55 for epoxiconazole.
A more detailed description of the experiment procedure is available in protocols\2_EC50_tests and the temporality of all experiments is described in a GANTT chart Section 1.2.2.


4.1.2 Experimental results
Variables names :

Date : Date of the measurement
ID_cosm : Identification number of the cosm
t : Number of days since the start of the exposition (d)
w_tot : Fresh weight of the earthworms in one cosm (mg)
Nb_ind : Number of alive individuals in a cosm (#)
Dose : concentration in the soil (mg/kg)

“J” : Juvenile
“A” : Adulte
“D” : Dead

4.1.2.2 Dose-response model
Dose-response curves are modeled with the Hill model (Equation 4.1, Figure 4.2).
\[
Y=Y_{min}+\frac{Y_{max}-Y_{min}}{1+\text{exp}(Slope\times [\text{Ln}(Dose)-\text{Ln}(EC_{50})])}
\tag{4.1}\]
With :

\(Y\) : Response for a given dose,
\(Y_{min}\) : Minimal response,
\(Y_{max}\) : Maximal response,
\(EC_{50}\) : Dose for which the response equals \((Y_{max}-Y_{min})/2\),
\(Slope\) : Slope when the dose equals the EC\(_{50}\).









Figure 4.2: Schematic representation of a dose-response curve with the Hill model

4  Effects of single exposures on earthworms

title: 4  Effects of single exposures on earthworms
text:
4.2 Juvenile growth

4.2.1 Growth experiment
Juveniles used in these tests were collected in the culture with similar body weights. Juvenile growth tests followed the same pattern as reproduction tests. The study of the effects of individual pesticides was performed using the same doses as in the reproduction tests.
For each replicate, one earthworm was placed in a cosm consisting of a plastic vessel (11 cm × 7.7 cm × 4.5 cm) containing the equivalent of 200 g of dry soil. The exposure lasted 28 days at 18°C. Earthworms were weighed at the start, after 14 days and at the end of the experiment (28 days) and were fed ad libitum with horse dung (3 g per individual every 14 days). Soil moisture was checked and adjusted weekly. At the end of the experiments, earthworms were starved on wet filter paper in Petri dishes to empty their gut contents before being frozen at -80°C.


4.2.2 Experimental results
Variables names :

Date : Date of the measurement
ID : Identification number of the earthworm
t : Number of days since the start of the exposition
w : Fresh weight of the earthworm (mg)
Dose : concentration in the soil (mg/kg)
status :

“J” : Juvenile
“A” : Adulte
“D” : Dead

4.2.3 Effect on juvenile growth

4.2.3.1 Growth model - Growth rates calculation
The growth model is the following :
\[
\frac{dL}{dt}=a \Rightarrow L(t)=L_0 + a\times t
\]
With :

L : The structural volumetric length of the earthworm (\(= \sqrt[3]{w}\)) (mg\(^{1/3}\))
a : Growth rate (mg\(^{1/3}\)/d)

For each earthworm, the growth rate is estimated using nls from the “stats” package.


Code
f_growth_rate <- function(data){
  a_init <- 0.1
  a_i <- c()
  
  # Calculation of the growth rate for each individual
  for(i in subset(data, t==0)$ID){
    data_i <- data.frame(
      L = subset(data, ID==i)$L,
      t = subset(data, ID==i)$t
      )
    L0_i <- subset(data, ID==i & t==0)$L
    
    if(length(na.omit(data_i$L))==2){ # If only 2 data points
      a.Est <- (subset(data_i, !t==0)$L-subset(data_i, t==0)$L)/
        subset(data_i, !t==0)$t
    }else{ # If 3 data points (or more)
      EPX.nlsHill=nls(
        L ~ L0_i+t*a,
        start = list(a=a_init), 
        trace=T, 
        data=data_i
        ) 
      a.Est <- EPX.nlsHill$m$getPars()[1]
    }
    a_i <- rbind(a_i, a.Est)
  }

  return(a_i)
}

text:
5.1 Graphical representations
Considering mixtures, there are 3 possible outcomes in terms of toxic effects :
In ecotoxicology, the last case in the most concerning one as security levels determined on single substances can be insufficient to protect the environment.
As seen in the last part, when only one substance is studied at a time it gives us dose-reponse curves (2D : Dose x Effect). But when we study a binary mixture, we are looking to define a dose-response surface (3D : Dose substance A x Dose substance B x Effect). This surface can be displayed in 3D but also in 2D, under the same principle of level line in maps (Figure 5.1).

title: 5  How to study a binary mixture ?
text:
5.2 Interaction model of Jonker, (2005)

5.2.1 General principle
To model the dose-response surface of the binary mixture, we can use the simple interaction model of Jonker et al. (2005). This model is based on the dose-response curves of the single substances and an interaction parameter, \(a\). This parameter explicitly quantifies how much the observed dose–response surface departs from the additivity baseline. This formalism has the advantage of being continuous: interaction strength and direction are measured on a single scale, which avoids the dichotomy between “interactive” and “non-interactive” mixtures.
Additivity (no interaction)
In case of no interaction (null hypothesis), this model define the null model as the model describing the dose-response surface in the case of no interaction between the two substances. This model is based on the concentration addition principle (CA) and in this case \(a\) = 0. Because effects are then additive, effect isobole, which describe the pairs of doses leading to the same given level of effect, are linear. For example, if we consider all pairs of doses leading to a 50% effect, each dose of a substance can be expressed as a fraction of its own EC\(_{50}\) and the additivity is verified if the sum of the two fractions are equal to 1.
Additivity is verified in the case where Equation 5.1 is verified :
\[\forall (C_A,C_B)=(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B)\ \text{ with }\ \text{ Effect}(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B) = 50\%,\ x+y=1 \tag{5.1}\]
Antagonism
In the case of antagonism, Equation 5.1 is not verified anymore and isoboles are concave with \(a\) > 0. For example, if we consider all pairs of doses leading to a 50% effect, each dose of a substance can be expressed as a fraction of its own EC\(_{50}\) and antagonism occurs if the sum of the two fractions are above 1. How above is quantified by \(a\). We need more of the mixture to get an effect of 50%.
\[\forall (C_A,C_B)=(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B)\ \text{ with }\ \text{ Effect}(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B) = 50\%,\ x+y>1 \tag{5.2}\]
Synergy
In the case of synergy, Equation 5.1 is also not verified and isoboles are convexe with \(a\) < 0. For example, if we consider all pairs of doses leading to a 50% effect, each dose of a substance can be expressed as a fraction of its own EC\(_{50}\) and antagonism occurs if the sum of the two fractions are below 1. How below is quantified by \(a\). We need less of the mixture to get an effect of 50%.
\[\forall (C_A,C_B)=(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B)\ \text{ with }\ \text{ Effect}(x\ EC_{50}^A\ ;\ y\ EC_{50}^B) = 50\%,\ x+y<1 \tag{5.3}\]
 

5.2.1.1 Other kinds of Jonker interaction models
Two other more sophisticated models were developped by Jonker introducing an second interaction parameter (\(b\)) :

The DL model : Take into account the fact that the interaction can depend on the level of effect.
The DR model : Take into account the fact that the interaction can depend on the ratio of the two substances in the mixture.




5.2.2 Formal mathematical definition

5.2.2.1 Simple interaction model
For a binary mixture, the simple interaction model can be writen as follows :
\[
\frac{c_1}{f^{-1}_1(Y)}+\frac{c_2}{f^{-1}_2(Y)}=\text{exp}(G)
\tag{5.4}\]
\[
G(z_1, z_2)=a\times (z_1\times z_2)
\tag{5.5}\]
And :
\[
z_i=\frac{\text{TU}_{x_i}}{\text{TU}_{x_1}+\text{TU}_{x_2}},\ \text{ where }\  \text{TU}_{x_i}=\frac{c_i}{EC_{x_i}}
\tag{5.6}\]
With :

\(Y\) : The response to a given couple of concentrations,
\(c_1\) & \(c_2\) the respective concentrations of substance 1 and 2,
\(f^{-1}\) : The inverse fonction of the dose-response relationship of substance 1 and 2,
\(x\) : 5, 10, or 50,
\(z_1\) & \(z_2\) : The respective contribution to the total effect of substance 1 and 2,
\(a\) : The interaction parameter (\(a\) < 0 if synergy, \(a\) > 0 if antagonism).



5.2.2.2 The DL model
In this case, \(G\) includes a second interaction parameter \(b\) :
\[
G(z_1, z_2)=a(1-b)\ z_1 z_2
\tag{5.7}\]
If \(b\) = 1, it will induces a switch from antagonism to synergism at the EC50 level. Other values for \(b\) will induces a switch at other effect levels.


5.2.2.3 The DR model
In this case, \(G\) also includes a second interaction parameter \(b\) :
\[
G(z_1, z_2)=(a+bz_1)\ z_1z_2
\tag{5.8}\]

\(b\) > 0 : Antagonism where the toxicity of the mixture is mainly caused by substance 1,
\(b\) < 0 : Synergism where the toxicity of the mixture is mainly caused by substance 1.




5.2.3 Computations
In practice, fitting the Jonker interaction model involves a two-step optimization:

Inner optimization (dose combination search) : For each pair of tested concentrations \((C_A, C_B)\) and for a given set of interaction parameters, the corresponding effects must be found numerically.
Outer optimization (interaction parameter estimation) : Once the effect surface is reconstructed across all data points, the interaction parameter \(a\) is estimated.

To perform the inner optimization, a function CA_complete2() was written. For a given set of interaction parameters, finding the corresponding effect for a couple of concentration (\(c_A\) ; \(c_B\)) implies the minimization of the following term :
\[
\frac{c_A}{f^{-1}_A(Y)}+\frac{c_B}{f^{-1}_B(Y)}-\text{exp}(G)
\tag{5.9}\]
For the outer optimization, a function CA_complete_fit_speed() was written. Parameter estimation for the interaction models requires maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The optimization procedure depends on the assumed error distribution: for normally distributed errors, this is equivalent to minimizing the residual sum of squares (calculated with the function CA_complete2_RSS()), while for Poisson-distributed errors, the log-likelihood function (Equation 5.12) (calculated with the function CA_complete2_Poisson()) is directly maximized.
Let \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n)\) be the vector of observed responses, \(\mathbf{\theta}\) the parameter vector to be estimated, and \(f(.|\mathbf{\theta})\) the density function conditional to the parameters. Then, the likelihood function is defined as :
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta | \mathbf{y})=\prod_{i=1}^nf(y_i|\theta)
\tag{5.10}\]
The log-likelihood function, which is computationally more tractable, is given by:
\[
l(\theta|\mathbf{y}) = \ln(\mathcal{L}(\theta | \mathbf{y})) = \sum^n_{i=1} \ln(f(y_i|\theta))\\
\tag{5.11}\]
For count data (cocoon production), assuming \(y_i \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda_i)\) where \(\lambda_i = g(\mathbf{x_i}; \theta)\) represents the expected response given covariates \(\mathbf{x_i}\), the log-likelihood becomes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
l(\theta|\mathbf{y}) &=\sum^n_{i=1} \ln\left( \frac{e^{-\lambda_i}\lambda_i^{y_i}}{y_i!}\right) \\
&= \sum^n_{i=1} [y_i \ln(\lambda_i) - \lambda_i - \ln(y_i!)]\\
&= \sum^n_{i=1} [y_i \ln(g(x_i;\theta)) - g(x_i;\theta) - \ln(y_i!)]
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.12}\]






Jonker, M. J., Svendsen, C., Bedaux, J. J. M., Bongers, M., & Kammenga, J. E. (2005). Significance testing of synergistic/antagonistic, dose level‐dependent, or dose ratio‐dependent effects in mixture dose‐response analysis. Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry, 24(10), 2701–2713. https://doi.org/10.1897/04-431R.1

title: 6  Experimental design construction for mixture effect on reproduction
text:
6.1 Tests of different joint dose-response model for EPX and IMD
To be able to study the mixture and based on the Jonker simple interaction model, we need to see if we can consider that the dose-response curves of each molecule have common maximums and common slopes. Therefore, we need to compare different dose-response models where certain parameters are fitted indepently or not.
Code
# Value given to controls for plot
Val_Ctrl <- 1e-4
Label_Ctrl <- "0 (Ctrl)"

# Data EC50

df_repro_tot <- read_excel(here::here("data/Data_EC50.xlsx"), sheet="Repro") |> 
  mutate(
    Dose = as.numeric(Dose),
    Dose_plot = case_when(
      Dose == 0 ~ Val_Ctrl,
      !(Dose == 0) ~ Dose
    ),
    Dose_f = as.factor(round(Dose, 4)),
    w=w_tot/Nb_ind,
    L=w^(1/3),
    )

# Data for EPX
df_repro_EPX <- subset(df_repro_tot, Molec %in% c("Ctrl_2", "EPX")) |> 
  mutate(Molecule = "EPX")
# We only keep earthworms still alive at then end of the experiment
ID_alive_EPX <- subset(df_repro_EPX, t==28 & (!Status=="D"))$ID_cosm
df_repro_EPX_alive <- subset(df_repro_EPX, ID_cosm %in% ID_alive_EPX)

# Data for IMD
df_repro_IMD <- subset(df_repro_tot, Molec %in% c("Ctrl_1", "Ctrl_2", "IMD")) |> 
  mutate(Molecule = "IMD")
# We only keep earthworms still alive at then end of the experiment
ID_alive_IMD <- subset(df_repro_IMD, t==28 & (!Status=="D"))$ID_cosm
df_repro_IMD_alive <- subset(df_repro_IMD, ID_cosm %in% ID_alive_IMD)

df_repro <- rbind(df_repro_EPX, df_repro_IMD)
df_repro_alive <- rbind(df_repro_EPX_alive, df_repro_IMD_alive)

Control_IMD <- mean(subset(df_repro_IMD_alive, Dose == 0)$Nb_cocoons, na.rm=T)
Control_EPX <- mean(subset(df_repro_EPX_alive, Dose == 0)$Nb_cocoons, na.rm=T)

df_repro_EPX_alive <- df_repro_EPX_alive |> 
  mutate(
    r_Nb_cocoons = Nb_cocoons / Control_EPX *100
    ) 
df_repro_IMD_alive <- df_repro_IMD_alive |> 
  mutate(
    r_Nb_cocoons = Nb_cocoons / Control_EPX * 100
    ) 


df_repro_alive <- df_repro_alive |> 
  mutate(
    r_Nb_cocoons = case_when(
      Molecule == "IMD" ~ Nb_cocoons / Control_IMD,
      Molecule == "EPX" ~ Nb_cocoons / Control_EPX
    ) * 100
    ) 

df_repro_alive_mean <- df_repro_alive |>
  dplyr::group_by(Dose, Dose_plot, Molecule) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Nb_cocoons = mean(Nb_cocoons, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_Nb_cocoons = mean(r_Nb_cocoons, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

  type="continuous",
  fct=LL.4(
    names = c("slope", "Ymin", "Ymax", "EC50"),
    fixed=c(NA, 0, NA, NA)
    ), 
    # Reproduction is expected to reach 0 for large concentrations

  )

6.2 Construction of the experimental design


Code
drc_res <- read.csv(here::here("data/DRC_parameters_cocoons_really_used.csv"), sep=",")

Y_max <- drc_res[2, 2]
Y_min <- 0
slope <- drc_res[1, 2]
EPX_EC50 <- drc_res[3, 2]
IMD_EC50 <- drc_res[4, 2]

EPX_drc <- function(dose){
  return(Y_min+(Y_max-Y_min)/(1+exp(slope*(log(dose)-log(EPX_EC50)))))
}

IMD_drc <- function(dose){
  Y_max <- drc_res[2, 2]
  Y_min <- 0
  slope <- drc_res[1, 2]
  EPX_EC50 <- drc_res[3, 2]
  IMD_EC50 <- drc_res[4, 2]
  return(Y_min+(Y_max-Y_min)/(1+exp(slope*(log(dose)-log(IMD_EC50)))))
}

max_dose_EPX <- max(subset(df_design, !EPX==0)$EPX)

library(bayestestR)
f_pdir <- function(df){
  Nb_rep_unique = unique(df$Nb_rep)
  Simulated_interaction_unique = unique(df$Simulated_interaction)
  
  res <- data.frame(
    Nb_rep = c(),
    Simulated_interaction = c(),
    P_direction = c())
  
  for(Nb_rep_i in Nb_rep_unique){
    for(Simulated_interaction_i in Simulated_interaction_unique){
      
      p_dir <- p_direction(subset(df, Nb_rep == Nb_rep_i & Simulated_interaction == Simulated_interaction_i)$Estimated_interaction)
      
      res_i <- data.frame(
    Nb_rep = Nb_rep_i,
    Simulated_interaction = Simulated_interaction_i,
    P_direction = p_dir[2])
      
      res <- rbind(res, res_i)
    }
  }
  return(res)
}

df_boot_res_line <- df_boot_res_line |>

f_power_design <- function(Nb_rep, l_interaction_a, Nb_pop, param){
  
  res <- data.frame()

  for (Nb_rep_j in Nb_rep){
    for (interaction_a_i in l_interaction_a){
    
      print(interaction_a_i)
      
      a_i <- interaction_a_i
      
      # Calculation of the theorical response
      res_CA_theorical_design_i <- CA_complete2(
        C_mat, 
        Max, Slopes, Ec50s, 
        interact="SA", 
        a=a_i
      )
    
      # We add the corresponding response to our design
      df_dose_rep_i <- df_design%>%
        mutate(rep_Y=res_CA_theorical_design_i)
    
      df_dose_rep_i <- df_dose_rep_i[,-c(1, 4)]
      
      for(k in 1:Nb_pop){
        
        set.seed(121212+k)
        ID_pop <- k
        # Population simulation 
        df_sim_data_k <- data.frame(
          Y=c(),
          EPX=c(),
          IMD=c()
          )
        
        for(i in 1:length(df_dose_rep_i$EPX)){
          
          Y_th <- df_dose_rep_i$rep_Y[i]
          Y_sim <- rpois(Nb_rep_j, Y_th)
          
          EPX <- rep(df_dose_rep_i$EPX[i], Nb_rep_j)
          IMD <- rep(df_dose_rep_i$IMD[i], Nb_rep_j)
          
          df_sim_data_j <- data.frame(
            Y_th=rep(Y_th, Nb_rep_j),
            Y_sim=Y_sim,
            EPX=EPX,
            IMD=IMD
            )
          df_sim_data_k <- rbind(df_sim_data_k, df_sim_data_j)
        }
        # Fit of the model 
        res_CA_SA_fit_k<-CA_complete2_fit_speed(
          C_mat=cbind(                      
            df_sim_data_k$EPX,                
            df_sim_data_k$IMD                 
            ),                              
          Response=df_sim_data_k$Y_sim,       
          interact="SA",                      
          param=param                         
          )
        res_a_k <- res_CA_SA_fit_k$a
      
        res_k <- data.frame(
          Simulated_interaction = a_i,
          Estimated_interaction = res_a_k,
          ID_pop = ID_pop,
          Nb_rep = Nb_rep_j
          )
        res <- rbind(res, res_k)
      }
      
      
      print("Calculations done for given interaction")
      
    }
    print("Calculations done for given Nb_rep")
  }
  
  return(res)
}

9.3 Is the effect of single molecules the same in experiment A as in experiment B ?
To judge the reproducibility between the experiments, we need to compare the dose-response curves for EPX & IMD obtained with the experiment A and the experiment B (Autumn 2024 vs. Spring 2025).
Considering the inter-batch variability observed in control treatments, we standardized all responses by expressing them relative to the corresponding batch control. It gives us r_Nb_cocoons.

9.3.1 Comparison of the controls


Code
df_mix_coc_ctrl <- subset(df_mix_coc, Ratio == "N") |> 
  dplyr::select(Nb_cocoons) |> 
  mutate(Experiment = "Experiment B")

    Lot == "A" ~ "Experiment A\nSpring 2024",

9.3.2 Experiment A - Dose-response curves
We then get the dose-response curves of the single substances from experiment A and experiment B.


Code
Dose_x <- expand.grid(
  exp(
    seq(
      log(0.0001),log(5000),
      by=(log(5000)-log(0.0001))/100
    )
  )
)

drc.ExpA<- drm(
  Nb_cocoons~Dose, Molecule, 
  data = df_repro_alive,
  type="Poisson",
  fct=LL.4(
    names = c("slope", "Ymin", "Ymax", "EC50"),
    fixed = c(NA, 0, NA, NA)
  ), 
  # Reproduction is expected to reach 0 for large concentrations
  pmodels=data.frame(Molecule, Molecule, Molecule)
)

CI.ExpA <- data.frame(
  Dose = c(Dose_x$Var1, Dose_x$Var1),
  Molecule = c(rep("EPX", length(Dose_x$Var1)), rep("IMD", length(Dose_x$Var1)))
)

pm.ExpA <- predict(drc.ExpA, newdata=CI.ExpA, interval="confidence")
CI.ExpA$p <- pm.ExpA[,1]
CI.ExpA$pmin <- pm.ExpA[,2]
CI.ExpA$pmax <- pm.ExpA[,3]

EPX_EC50_ExpA <- coef(drc.ExpA)[5]
IMD_EC50_ExpA <- coef(drc.ExpA)[6]

summary(drc.ExpA)

Hill.mix.IE <- function(Dose, Molecule){
  
  i <- 0
  if(Molecule == "IMD"){i <- 1}
  
  Y_min <- 0
  slope <- coef(drc.mix.IE)[1]
  Y_max <- coef(drc.mix.IE)[2]
  EC50 <- coef(drc.mix.IE)[3+i]
  
  return(Y_min+(Y_max-Y_min)/(1+exp(slope*(log(Dose)-log(EC50)))))
}

# Calculation of the equivalent doses of the mono-substances that would give the said effect

f_dose_eq <- function(model, resp) {
  out <- tryCatch(
    ED(model, as.numeric(resp), type = "absolute", interval = "delta"),
    error = function(e) matrix(NA, nrow = 4, ncol = 2) # si erreur
  )

  m <- as.matrix(out)

  # Si moins de 4 lignes → compléter avec NA
  if (nrow(m) < 4) {
    m <- rbind(m, matrix(NA, nrow = 4 - nrow(m), ncol = ncol(m)))
  }

  tibble(
    Dose_eq_IMD       = m[1, 2],
    Dose_eq_EPX       = m[1, 1],
    Dose_eq_IMD_lower = m[3, 2],
    Dose_eq_EPX_lower = m[3, 1],
    Dose_eq_IMD_upper = m[4, 2],
    Dose_eq_EPX_upper = m[4, 1]
  )
}

calculate_predobs_stats <- function(df) {
  df <- df |> 
    mutate(
      Ratio_predobs = Predicted / Response,
      Residuals = Predicted - Response
    )
  
  per_fold2 <- mean(df$Ratio_predobs >= 0.5 & df$Ratio_predobs <= 2) * 100
  per_fold5 <- mean(df$Ratio_predobs >= 0.2 & df$Ratio_predobs <= 5) * 100
  
  list(df = df, per_fold2 = per_fold2, per_fold5 = per_fold5)
}


dfs <- list(
  CA = df_predobs_CA, SA = df_predobs_CASA, DL = df_predobs_CADL, DR = df_predobs_CADR,
  IA = df_predobs_IA, "IA-SA" = df_predobs_IASA, "IA-DL" = df_predobs_IADL, "IA-DR" = df_predobs_IADR
)

results <- lapply(dfs, calculate_predobs_stats)

df_predobs_summary <- data.frame(
  Reference_model = c(rep("CA", 4), rep("IA", 4)),
  Model = names(dfs),
  Per_fold2 = sapply(results, `[[`, "per_fold2"),
  Per_fold5 = sapply(results, `[[`, "per_fold5")

f_growth_rate <- function(data){
  a_init <- 0.1
  a_i <- c()
  
  # Calculation of the growth rate for each individual
  for(i in subset(data, t==0)$ID_cosm){
    data_i <- data.frame(L = subset(data, ID_cosm==i)$L,
                         t = subset(data, ID_cosm==i)$t)
    L0_i <- subset(data, ID_cosm==i & t==0)$L
    if(length(na.omit(data_i$L))==2){ # If only 2 data points
      a.Est <- (subset(data_i, !t==0)$L-subset(data_i, t==0)$L)/
        subset(data_i, !t==0)$t
    }else{
      a.Est <- NA
    }
    a_i <- rbind(a_i, a.Est)
  }
  return(a_i)
}

    names = c("slope", "Ymin", "Ymax", "EC50"),

pm.4 <- predict(drc.4, newdata=CI.4, interval="confidence")
CI.4$p <- pm.4[,1]
CI.4$pmin <- pm.4[,2]
CI.4$pmax <- pm.4[,3]

Hill.4 <- function(Dose, Molecule){
  
  i <- 0
  if(Molecule == "IMD"){i <- 1}
  
  Y_min <- 0
  slope <- coef(drc.4)[1]
  Y_max <- coef(drc.4)[2]
  EC50 <- coef(drc.4)[3+i]
  
  return(Y_min+(Y_max-Y_min)/(1+exp(slope*(log(Dose)-log(EC50)))))
}

IMD_EC50 <- coef(drc.4)[4]

Calculation of growth rates :


Code
f_growth_rate <- function(data){
  a_init <- 0.1
  a_i <- c()
  
  # Calculation of the growth rate for each individual
  for(i in subset(data, t==0)$ID){
    data_i <- data.frame(L = subset(data, ID==i)$L,
                         t = subset(data, ID==i)$t)
    L0_i <- subset(data, ID==i & t==0)$L
    if(length(na.omit(data_i$L))==2){ # If only 2 data points
      a.Est <- (subset(data_i, !t==0)$L-subset(data_i, t==0)$L)/
        subset(data_i, !t==0)$t
    }else{
      a.Est <- NA
    }
    a_i <- rbind(a_i, a.Est)
  }
  return(a_i)
}

10.4.5 Observations on hatchlings
A few observations could be made while monitoring hatchlings :

Usually, Aporrectodea caliginosa gives only one hatchling per cocoon. Here, it happened a few times that there were two. Each time it was seen, one very small earthworm was with a more normal weight earthworm. All occurence could not be witnessed as we could not observe all cocoons hatch.
Some hatchlings were really small (?fig-smallhatch), probably because of the previous point but it could also have happened in cocoons resulting in only one individual.
A small number of hatchlings were with malformations like two bodies (happenned, twice, ?fig-twobodieshatch), or anormal masses (happened twice, ?fig-cancerhatch).
